<reason>Both sides built a coherent, well-framed case, but A's rebuttals did more damage. A preempted the obvious "not comprehensive enough" reply by citing Mexico's national, escape-hatch-free soda tax and the UK sugar levy, and B never squarely answered either: B's rebuttal on "miniature" policies never engaged Mexico at all, and B's reformulation defense of the UK levy was directly rebutted by A's compensation-effect point (childhood obesity rose despite reformulation) — a rebuttal B's closing simply didn't revisit. A's pressure question also extracted a real concession (no jurisdiction shows environmental success), which A then leveraged effectively in closing ("universal coverage of a null effect is not reach"). B's equity/reach framing was genuinely strong and its closing reframe was rhetorically elegant, and B did land good pressure questions on funding and timeline double standards, which A answered reasonably (schools as a universal, non-enrollment channel; DPP's ~3-year outcome window). But B's failure to close the loop on its own flagship examples' null weight effects left A's strongest empirical line standing largely unanswered at the end. A's two clipped turns are a real execution cost, but the substantive content of both speeches still came through before the cutoff.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's rebuttal1 introduction of Mexico's national, no-escape-hatch soda tax and Britain's reformulation-yet-rising-obesity data, combined with A's follow-up "compensation effect" point in rebuttal2 — both of which B never directly rebutted — was the most decisive exchange, since it undercut B's core empirical claim that environmental policy demonstrably works once deployed at scale.</best_rebuttal>
